scoreNote: Strong (5): rejects the claim by exposing the reason as an unfalsifiable redefinition of self-interest that confuses an act's byproduct with its motive, then points to genuine self-sacrifice as decisive counter-evidence; addresses claim and reason.

sentences.text: When a stranger dives into a freezing river to save a drowning child, are we really to believe he did it for himself?
The claim says we must, asserting that no act is ever done purely for the benefit of others, on the reason that all actions, even apparently selfless ones, are based on self-interest.

The claim is mistaken, and its reason rests on a trick: by defining self-interest so broadly that it swallows everything, the argument makes itself impossible to disprove, while genuine self-sacrifice shows that purely other-directed acts do exist.

sections.role: Body — The reason cannot be disproved

sentences.text: The reason wins only by cheating, stretching self-interest until the word means almost nothing.

When someone sacrifices for others and feels satisfaction, the egoist says he acted for that satisfaction; if he feels nothing, the egoist says he acted to avoid guilt, so there is no possible act the theory cannot explain away.
But a claim that no evidence could ever refute is not a profound truth; it is an empty one, true only because it has been made unfalsifiable by definition.
An argument that counts every act as selfish, no matter what, has explained nothing about our real motives.

sections.role: Body — It confuses byproduct with motive

sentences.text: Moreover, the reason confuses the byproducts of an act with its purpose.
That a kind act also brings the doer pleasure does not show that pleasure was the goal, since the satisfaction may simply be the natural result of caring genuinely about someone else.
A parent who feeds her child before herself feels good because she loves the child, not the other way around, so her motive is the child's good and her own feeling a mere consequence.
We do not say a doctor heals patients merely for the salary because she is paid; the payment accompanies the work without being its point.
To insist that the feeling must be the real aim is to assume the very thing in question, reversing cause and effect to protect the theory.
Benefiting from a good act is not the same as doing it for that benefit.
Most decisively, there are acts that cannot be squared with self-interest at all.
A soldier who throws himself on a grenade to save his comrades gains nothing and loses everything, including the very self that self-interest is supposed to serve.
An anonymous donor who will never be thanked, or a stranger who helps at real cost and walks away, acts for others with no benefit left to collect.
Such acts are rare, but they need only exist to refute a claim that no act is ever purely for others, since a single genuine sacrifice is enough.
Pure altruism may be uncommon, but it is plainly real.
In conclusion, both the claim and its reason fail.

The reason saves itself only by defining self-interest so loosely that nothing could ever count against it, and it mistakes the pleasant byproduct of a generous act for its motive, while genuine self-sacrifice proves that some acts truly are done purely for the benefit of others.
We are not always selfish; sometimes we act, simply and wholly, for someone else.
